title: Observed use: Capability predictions exceed workplace adoption
desc: Uses task-level evidence to separate automation, augmentation and job redesign, with reliability and human planning limiting transformation.

kps.k: Task-level AI use provides evidence of changing work, not a direct measure of jobs displaced.
kps.d: This cluster distinguishes theoretical capability, observed adoption, successful task completion and employment outcomes. Anthropic’s observed-exposure measure combines theoretical feasibility with professional Claude usage, weights automation more heavily than augmentation, and accounts for task time. Its January effective-coverage measure instead weights task success by time and frequency. Neither establishes how much human work disappears. The Economic Index dashboard also explicitly classifies conversation content, not users’ actual occupations.

qs.q: ### A new measure of occupational exposure  Our new measure, observed exposure*, is meant to quantify: of those tasks that LLMs could theoretically speed up, which are actually seeing automated usage in professional settings?
qs.a: Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: It’s calculated as the weighted sum of task success rates, where each task's weight is its share of the worker's time adjusted by how frequently the task occurs.
qs.a: Anthropic Economic Index Report: Economic Primitives (January 2026) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Predicted capability substantially exceeds observed adoption, leaving the pace of transformation uncertain.
kps.d: Labor market impacts of AI reports 94% theoretical exposure for Computer and Math tasks but only 33% observed Claude coverage. Economic Evaluations of Language Models finds minimal or no Claude usage for 79.4% of tasks with predicted time savings of at least 25%. The authors propose model limitations, legal constraints, verification, software integration and complementary organisational changes as explanations. These gaps indicate potential applications, not realised savings; missing usage on one platform does not establish either technical impossibility or absence of adoption elsewhere.

qs.q: For example, the β measure shows scope for LLM penetration in the majority of tasks in Computer & Math (94%) and Office & Admin (90%) occupations.
qs.a: Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: However, among tasks where AI can save at least 25% of time, 79.4% (5681/7159) have minimal to no Claude usage.
qs.a: Economic Evaluations of Language Models · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Employment evidence distinguishes automation from augmentation rather than supporting a uniform displacement account.
kps.d: Evaluating the Impact of AI on the Labor Market reports stable employment shares across relative exposure groups since ChatGPT’s launch and no clear upward trend in exposed tasks among unemployed workers’s previous occupations. The August 2026 Canaries revision reports contrasting associations: automation-oriented use is consistent with labour substitution, while complementary use accompanies flat or rising employment; the highest augmentation quintile has among the fastest young-worker employment growth. These findings concern different measures and populations, not a clean contradiction. The supplied Canaries excerpts do not identify the employment observation window, and neither account establishes causation.

qs.q: The share of workers in the lowest, middle, and highest occupational exposure groups stay stable at around 29%, 46% and 18%, respectively.
qs.a: Evaluating the Impact of AI on the Labor Market: Current State of Affairs · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Employment changes for young  workers are not ordered by complementarity exposure, as the fifth quintile has among the fastest  employment growth.
qs.a: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence (August 2026 revision) · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Agentic execution can expand while human planning and domain expertise remain important.
kps.d: Agentic Coding and Persistent Returns to Expertise analyses roughly 400,000 interactive sessions from October 2025 to April 2026. Users typically make 70% of planning decisions while Claude makes 80% of execution decisions. Inferred task-specific expertise correlates with more activity, better outcomes and easier error recovery, although experts’ advantage over intermediate users is modest. Separately, the March Learning Curves report finds that longer-tenure users collaborate more and achieve higher model-assessed success, reversing Anthropic’s earlier hypothesis that sophisticated users would favour automation. Selection, cohort effects and survivorship prevent a causal interpretation of learning-by-doing; the coding study also excludes much programmatic use.

qs.q: This report provides evidence on how Claude Code is used in practice, based on a [privacy-preserving analysis](https://www.anthropic.com/research/clio) of ~400,000 interactive sessions from ~235,000 people between October 2025 and April 2026.
qs.a: Agentic Coding and Persistent Returns to Expertise · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: This pushes back against a hypothesis we made last year that automated use may be more typical of more experienced, sophisticated users; instead, we find that the most advanced users are more likely to iterate with Claude.
qs.a: Anthropic Economic Index Report: Learning Curves (March 2026) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Reliability and remaining human tasks limit productivity gains, while job redesign creates competing skill scenarios.
kps.d: Anthropic’s January model lowers additional annual productivity growth over a decade from 1.8 percentage points to 1.2 for chat and 1.0 for API use after discounting time savings by model-assessed success. This adjustment addresses reliability but does not directly measure verification costs; results also depend on task thresholds and aggregation assumptions. Mechanically removing AI-covered tasks predicts net deskilling across most occupations. McCrory instead emphasises reorganising jobs around complementary expertise and remaining human tasks. These are alternative conditional mechanisms, not measured wage effects, and he acknowledges that stronger agents could eventually diminish returns to expertise.

qs.q: When σ<1 (complements), productivity gains are bottlenecked by tasks with the smallest speedups.
qs.a: Anthropic Economic Index Report: Economic Primitives (January 2026) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: Such empowerment from AI may redraw the boundaries of our roles, and produce new bundlings of tasks within jobs—automating some, reinforcing the importance of others—while on net increasing the marginal product of labor.
qs.a: Peter McCrory on X: 'Why hasn't AI increased unemployment?' — Anthropic's head of economics synthesises 18 months of research into a skill-biased, labor-augmenting framework for why AI has produced no material rise in US unemployment · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Reported benefits coexist with displacement anxiety, and legal-sector evidence remains mixed and limited.
kps.d: The April 2026 study of roughly 81,000 voluntary Claude respondents finds that, among those explicitly mentioning productivity, 48% cite broader scope and 40% speed. One fifth voice displacement concerns, with early-career respondents more anxious. Legal and scientific workers report the mildest productivity improvements, and some lawyers question instruction-following. Meanwhile, the coding study identifies legal occupations among its fastest-growing non-software groups. Growth in inferred usage and modest self-reported benefits measure different things; neither establishes legal-sector productivity or employment effects. The survey’s self-selection, open-ended responses and classifier-inferred attributes make its findings exploratory.

qs.q: We find that the most common productivity enhancement is in scope, which was cited by 48% of users who explicitly mentioned productivity effects.
qs.a: What 81,000 people told us about the economics of AI · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: The fastest-growing non-software occupation groups in our sample are management, sales, and legal occupations.
qs.a: Agentic Coding and Persistent Returns to Expertise · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Platform selection and measurement choices materially change apparent exposure.
kps.d: Evaluating the Impact of AI on the Labor Market finds that assigning zero usage to unobserved tasks, rather than excluding them, reduces estimated employment shares in high-automation and high-augmentation occupations from about 70% and 11% to 3% and 0%. Chat conversations, isolated API calls and complete agent sessions also capture different units of work. Google’s ATLAS adds evidence of disproportionate computer, business and creative task use across its own products, but does not make Claude data representative. Reuse of Economic Index data across reports and McCrory’s synthesis should not count as independent corroboration.

qs.q: The proportion of employment in occupations with high levels of task AI usage, whether automation or augmentation (as defined as more than half of AI usage), is stable at around 70% or 11%, respectively (Figure 15).
qs.a: Evaluating the Impact of AI on the Labor Market: Current State of Affairs · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Part of this reflects the nature of the interaction: Claude.ai transcripts can include multi-turn conversations, while the API data we analyze is limited to single input-output pairs.
qs.a: Anthropic Economic Index Report: Economic Primitives (January 2026) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Practical implications centre on complementary skills, workflow redesign and better outcome measurement.
kps.d: The sources recommend developing effective-use skills alongside access, adapting organisational practices and sharing privacy-protected individual, enterprise and API data across providers. Anthropic warns that learning advantages could reinforce inequality rather than diffuse automatically: its March report lengthens the conditional US adoption-convergence projection from 2–5 to 5–9 years and reports increasing international concentration. For employers and policymakers, the research supports tracking verification effort, successful workflow completion and employment outcomes separately from usage volume, predicted savings and user sentiment.

qs.q: For AI to benefit users globally, expanding access alone will not suffice—developing the human capital that enables effective use, particularly in lower-income economies, is essential.
qs.a: Anthropic Economic Index Report: Economic Primitives (January 2026) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: The countries using Claude the most (per capita) now account for a larger share of overall usage, with the top 20 countries going from 45 to 48% of usage adjusted for population.
qs.a: Anthropic Economic Index Report: Learning Curves (March 2026) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: The curated legal-tech-vendor sources accept the proposition that task-level AI capability and usage should not be equated with workplace adoption, successful performance, productivity or job displacement. They also materially develop it by supplying distinct measurement frameworks: observed exposure combines theoretical feasibility with professional usage; effective coverage incorporates task success, time and frequency; agentic-session analysis separates human planning from AI execution; and Gemini data broadens the evidence beyond Claude. Common reasons for caution include platform and sample boundaries, uneven occupational adoption, model limitations, legal and software constraints, human verification, reliability, complementary tasks and the continued value of domain expertise. Internal variation concerns where transformation appears most advanced and how it may unfold. API and agentic workflows suggest increasing automation or implementation capacity, while experienced users often collaborate and retain planning authority. Some modelling predicts deskilling or lower labour demand under task-removal assumptions, whereas other findings suggest expertise remains complementary. Legal-sector signals are especially unsettled: inferred legal use is growing in agentic coding, but surveyed legal workers report comparatively mild productivity gains. These are differing indicators rather than direct contradictions, and none establishes realised legal-sector employment effects.

vlens.an: The supplied market-analyst/press voice, represented here only by Peter McCrory and not as evidence of the wider group’s prevalence, accepts the synthesis’s central distinction between task capability and job displacement. McCrory materially extends it with a mechanism for job redesign: because automation remains incomplete, non-automated tasks, human planning and domain expertise can complement AI execution, changing task bundles rather than eliminating whole occupations. His account also aligns with the synthesis’s emphasis on reliability limits and the difference between observed use and expectations: survey forecasts of extensive automation are treated as expectations, while current usage evidence suggests expanded scope and changing responsibilities rather than demonstrated economy-wide employment effects. The principal internal variation is temporal. McCrory presents labour augmentation and persistent returns to expertise as the current pattern, but not a durable law; more autonomous and uniformly capable agents could weaken complementarity and reduce returns to human expertise. That forward-looking qualification preserves the synthesis’s uncertainty rather than opposing its present-tense proposition.

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources support the proposition that predicted AI capability and task exposure exceed realised workplace adoption and cannot be translated directly into job displacement. Their common reasoning is that capability, use and labour-market outcomes are distinct stages: potentially valuable tasks may show little observed Claude use; exposure groups can remain stable in employment even as AI use develops; and employment patterns differ between automation-oriented and complementary uses. They also consistently qualify inference: Claude usage is not representative of economy-wide adoption, missing-task assumptions materially alter exposure estimates, and reported employment relationships are associations rather than demonstrated causal effects. Material internal variation lies in emphasis rather than direction. Economic Evaluations of Language Models directly documents the capability–adoption gap and attributes it to complementary workflows, skills and organisational practices. Evaluating the Impact of AI on the Labor Market emphasises stable aggregate indicators and measurement sensitivity. Canaries in the Coal Mine distinguishes automation, which is consistent with labour substitution, from augmentation, which accompanies flat or rising employment. Thus, these sources support uncertainty about the pace and employment effects of transformation rather than claiming that AI has no displacement potential. Because the corpus is curated, this assessment characterises only the supplied research sources and not academia or researchers generally.

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the proposition that predicted AI capability and task exposure should not be treated as workplace adoption or realised labour-market transformation. It finds no change since ChatGPT’s launch in employment shares across relative exposure groups and no clear increase in AI-exposed prior occupations among unemployed workers. Its main explanatory contribution is methodological: apparent adoption at scale varies sharply with how missing tasks are handled, and Claude usage is skewed toward particular occupational content rather than representative of economy-wide use. Internal variation lies in the estimates rather than the overall conclusion: excluding unobserved tasks produces high apparent automation and augmentation shares, while assigning those tasks zero usage reduces the estimates dramatically. The source therefore treats current provider metrics as useful but imperfect proxies and calls for privacy-protected usage data across providers, enterprises and APIs before drawing stronger conclusions about adoption or displacement.

qs.q: When assuming that unobserved tasks indicate zero usage, however, these proportions drop to 3% and 0%, respectively.
qs.a: Evaluating the Impact of AI on the Labor Market: Current State of Affairs · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Our analysis shows that it has not (Figure 11).

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources accept the proposition’s core distinction between predicted capability, observed task use, successful completion and employment effects, while materially developing it in several directions. Common reasons are that platform usage is bounded and uneven; theoretical time savings greatly exceed observed adoption; reliability, verification, integration and organisational change constrain realised gains; and agentic execution often leaves planning and quality control with humans. The evidence also extends beyond Claude through Gemini task-use data and distinguishes automation-oriented use, associated with labour substitution, from augmentation, associated with flat or rising employment. Material internal variation concerns mechanism and trajectory rather than the core proposition: some modelling predicts deskilling when higher-skill tasks are removed, whereas coding and learning evidence finds persistent returns to domain expertise and collaborative use; legal occupations show growing inferred coding-agent usage but comparatively mild self-reported productivity benefits; and McCrory warns that current complementarity may weaken as agents improve. These are conditional estimates, associations and user reports rather than established economy-wide displacement or productivity effects, and the selected sources should not be treated as representative of broader stakeholder groups.
